cards.narration: Mia's soccer team orders one pizza for after the game. The whole pizza is one whole.
The pizza is cut into 8 equal slices. The bottom number of a fraction tells how many equal parts make one whole.
Mia eats 3 slices. The top number counts the parts we mean. She ate 3 of the 8 slices. That is 3/8 of the pizza.
Dev has a chocolate bar with 5 equal pieces. He eats 2 of them. That is 2/5 of the bar.
Think of 2/5 as one fifth added two times. The bottom number sets the size of each piece. The top number counts the pieces.
Sometimes the top number is bigger than the bottom number. Two pans are each cut into 4 pieces. Each piece is one fourth. Five pieces are picked. That is 5/4.
Now it is your turn. Tap, type, or move the frog to match each fraction.
Sam has a chocolate bar. He shares it equally with one friend. That makes 2 people, so each gets 1/2.
Next, Sam shares a bar of the same size with 3 friends. That is 4 people. Each person gets 1/4.
Compare the two shares. One half is bigger than one fourth. When more people share, each share gets smaller.
The bottom number tells how many people share. A bigger bottom number means a smaller share. Here is 1/6 of a pizza.
Be careful. The wholes must be the same size. We only compare shares when the pizzas or bars match in size.
Now put shares in order. Sharing by 6 gives the least. Sharing by 3 is more. Sharing by 2 gives the most.
You know the secret now. More sharers means a smaller share. Let's practise comparing fair shares.
Jay has a chocolate bar. It is cut into 4 equal pieces. Each piece is one fourth of the bar. We call one fourth 1/4.
Jay eats one piece. Then he eats another. Now count the pieces: 1 one fourth, 2 one fourths. That is 2/4 of the bar.
He keeps counting. 3 one fourths, then 4 one fourths. Four fourths fill the whole bar. So 4/4 is 1 whole.
Jay's friend brings a second bar, also cut in fourths. Keep counting. 5 one fourths. That is 5/4, which is more than 1 whole.
Adding 1/4 again and again is the same as multiplying. Three one fourths added up is 3 × 1/4. That equals 3/4. The number of pieces goes on top.
Now try pizza cut in thirds. Count 5 one thirds. That is 5 × 1/3, or 5/3. It is 1 whole pizza and 2 more thirds.
You can count by halves, thirds, fourths, and more, even past 1 whole. Let's practise!
Sam is getting ready for soccer. He has one water jug. The jug is one whole. Sam splits it into 10 equal parts. Each part is one tenth.
Sam fills 6 of the 10 parts. That is 6 tenths. As a decimal, it looks like 0.6.
The dot is called the decimal point. The 0 before it means no whole jugs. The first digit after the dot counts tenths.
Now Sam fills 1 whole jug and 4 more tenths. That is 1 and 4 tenths. It looks like 1.4. The 1 counts wholes. The 4 counts tenths.
To compare, look at the wholes first. 3.2 is less than 5.1, because 3 is less than 5.
If the wholes match, compare the tenths. 24.7 is greater than 24.3, because 7 tenths is more than 3 tenths.
A zero in the tenths place means no tenths. So 5.0 is the same as 5. Now let's practise with Sam!
Sam is building a fence. One whole fence has 10 boards. Here are the 10 boards.
Sam paints 1 board. That is 1 out of 10. We call it one tenth. As a fraction it is 1/10. As a decimal it is 0.1.
Now Sam has painted 5 boards. That is 5 tenths. It is 5/10, or 0.5. It is also one half of the fence!
Sam paints all 10 boards. That is 10 tenths. It makes 1 whole fence. As a decimal, it is 1.0.
Next, Sam paints 15 boards across two fences. That is 15 tenths. It is 1 whole fence and 5 tenths more. As a decimal, it is 1.5.
Here is the trick. The first digit after the dot counts tenths. So 0.3 is 3 tenths, and 3/10 is the same amount.
Now you can match fractions and decimals. Let's practise with Sam's fences!
Sam collects sports cards. Each pack has 6 cards. He knows his fives, so 5 packs is 5 × 6 = 30 cards.
Sam buys one more pack. That adds 6 more cards. So 6 × 6 is 30 plus 6, which is 36. Add one more set!
Now Sam has 4 packs of 7 cards. He knows 2 × 7 is 14. Four packs is double that. Double 14 is 28.
Three packs of 4 cards? Start with 2 × 4, which is 8. Then add one more 4. That makes 12.
Sam shares 42 cards into packs of 6. He knows 7 × 6 is 42. So 42 ÷ 6 is 7 packs.
A times fact and a divide fact are partners. Use facts you know to find new ones. Let's practise!

items.narration: A pizza is cut into 4 equal slices. Mia eats 3 of them. What fraction of the pizza did she eat? Is it 3/4, 1/4, or 4/4?
items.why: The pizza has 4 equal slices, so the bottom number is 4. Mia ate 3 slices, so the top number is 3. That is 3/4.

items.narration: A pizza is cut into 6 equal slices. Two slices are picked. How many equal slices make the whole pizza?
items.prompt: How many equal slices in the whole?
items.why: Count every slice, picked or not. The whole pizza has 6 equal slices, and that is the bottom number.

items.narration: The line goes from 0 to 1 and is cut into 4 equal steps. Move the frog to 1/4.
items.why: The line is cut into fourths. One fourth is the first step after 0.

items.narration: Which circle has 1/3 picked? Is it 2 of 3 parts picked, 1 of 3 parts picked, or 1 of 2 parts picked?
items.why: Thirds mean 3 equal parts. One third has 1 of those 3 parts picked.

items.narration: A chocolate bar has 5 equal pieces. Dev eats 2 of them. What number goes on top of the fraction?
items.why: The top number counts the pieces we mean. Dev ate 2 pieces, so the top number is 2.

items.narration: A fraction strip has 10 equal parts. Seven parts are picked. What fraction is picked? Is it 7/10, 3/10, 10/7, or 7/3?
items.why: The strip has 10 equal parts, so the bottom number is 10. Seven are picked, so the top number is 7. That is 7/10.

items.narration: A pan of brownies has 8 equal pieces. The team ate 3 of them. How many pieces are left?
items.why: The whole pan has 8 pieces and 3 were eaten. Take 3 away from 8 to get 5 pieces left.

items.narration: The line goes from 0 to 1 and is cut into 10 equal steps. Move the frog to 7/10.
items.why: Each step is one tenth. Count 7 steps from 0 to land on 7/10.

items.narration: In the fraction 3/5, the bottom number is 5. What does it tell us? Is it parts in the whole, parts we are counting, or number of wholes?
items.why: The bottom number tells how many equal parts make one whole. The top number is the one that counts parts.

items.narration: Which rectangle shows 3/8? Is it 5 of 8 parts picked, 3 of 5 parts picked, or 3 of 8 parts picked?
items.why: Eighths mean 8 equal parts in the whole. Three eighths has 3 of those 8 parts picked.

items.narration: Two pizzas are each cut into 4 equal slices. Five slices are picked. That makes a fraction with 4 on the bottom. What number is on top?
items.why: The top number counts all the picked fourths. There are 4 in the first pizza and 1 in the second, so 5 fourths.

items.narration: Two pans are each cut into 3 equal pieces. Each piece is one third. Four pieces are picked. How many thirds are picked? Is it 4/3, 3/4, 3/3, or 1/3?
items.why: Each piece is one third, so the bottom number is 3. Four pieces are picked, so the top number is 4. That is 4/3.

items.narration: The line goes from 0 to 2 and is cut into fourths. Move the frog to 5/4.
items.why: Each step is one fourth. Count 5 steps from 0. You pass 1 whole at 4 steps, then go one more.

items.narration: 3 granola bars are shared equally by 4 people. How much does each person get? Is it 3/4, 4/3, 1/4, or 3/3?
items.why: Cut each bar into 4 equal pieces. Each person takes one piece from each of the 3 bars. That is 3 fourths, or 3/4.

items.narration: Add one tenth nine times. The bottom number stays 10. What number is on top of the new fraction?
items.why: Each one tenth adds 1 to the top number. Nine of them make 9 tenths, so the top number is 9.

items.narration: Two pizzas are the same size. One is shared by 2 friends. The other is shared by 4 friends. Who gets more, 2 friends or 4 friends?
items.why: Fewer people sharing means bigger pieces. Each of 2 friends gets 1/2, which is more than 1/4.

items.narration: A pizza is cut into equal slices. One slice is picked. That slice is one friend's share. How many friends share the pizza?
items.why: Count all the equal slices. There are 4 slices, so 4 friends share the pizza.

items.narration: A chocolate bar is shared equally. Each friend gets 1/5 of the bar. Move the frog to the number of friends sharing.
items.why: The bottom number of the share is the number of friends. The share 1/5 means 5 friends.

items.narration: Two chocolate bars are the same size. Which share is bigger, 1/3 of the bar or 1/8 of the bar?
items.why: Sharing by 3 makes bigger pieces than sharing by 8. So 1/3 is the bigger share.

items.narration: A pizza is shared by 4 friends. Then the same pizza is shared by 8 friends instead. Is each share smaller, bigger, or the same?
items.why: More friends means more cuts. Each of 8 friends gets 1/8, which is smaller than 1/4.

items.narration: Mia and Leo have pizzas of the same size. Mia shares with 3 people. Leo shares with 6 people. Who gets less, Mia or Leo?
items.why: Mia gets 1/3 and Leo gets 1/6. More sharers means a smaller share, so Leo gets less.

items.narration: Four pans of brownies are the same size. Which share is the biggest: 1/5, 1/10, 1/2, or 1/4?
items.why: The smallest number of sharers gives the biggest share. Sharing by 2 gives 1/2, the biggest.

items.narration: Pizza A is shared by 2 friends. A pizza of the same size, pizza B, is shared by 6 friends. How many more friends share pizza B?
items.why: Pizza B has 6 sharers and pizza A has 2. Subtract: 6 - 2 = 4 more friends.

items.narration: A pan of 12 brownies is shared equally by 3 friends. Move the frog to how many brownies each friend gets.
items.why: Share 12 brownies into 3 equal groups. 12 ÷ 3 = 4 brownies each.

items.narration: Three same-size bars are shared by different numbers of friends. Which gives the smallest share: 4 friends, 5 friends, or 10 friends?
items.why: Shares are 1/4, 1/5, and 1/10. The most sharers gives the smallest piece, so 10 friends.

items.narration: Same-size pizzas are shared by 2, 4, and 8 friends. Which list goes from least to greatest: 1/8 then 1/4 then 1/2, or 1/2 then 1/4 then 1/8, or 1/4 then 1/8 then 1/2?
items.why: Most sharers gives the least. So the order is 1/8, then 1/4, then 1/2.

items.narration: One pizza is shared by 2 friends. Two pizzas of the same size are shared by 4 friends. Does each friend get the same amount, yes or no?
items.why: One pizza for 2 friends is 1/2 each. Two pizzas for 4 friends is also 2/4, which equals 1/2.

items.narration: Tia gets 1/2 of a bar. Ben gets 1/8 of the same bar. How many of Ben's shares fit in Tia's share?
items.why: The bar has 8 equal parts. Tia's half is 4 of them, so 4 of Ben's shares fit.

items.narration: A bar is cut into 10 equal parts for 10 friends. Move the frog to how many tenths make half of the bar.
items.why: Half of 10 equal parts is 5 parts. So 5/10 is the same as 1/2.

items.narration: Pizzas are all the same size. Which is the smallest share: 1/4 of the circle, 1/6 of the circle, 1/3 of the circle, or 1/10 of the circle?
items.why: The most sharers gives the smallest share. Sharing by 10 makes 1/10, the smallest piece.

items.narration: A pizza is cut into 4 equal slices. Three slices are picked. How many one fourths are picked? Is it 2, 3, 4, or 5?
items.why: Count the picked slices. There are 3 picked, so that is 3 one fourths, or 3/4.

items.narration: A chocolate bar is cut into 6 equal pieces. Five pieces are picked. How many one sixths are picked?
items.why: Count each picked piece. There are 5 picked pieces, so the answer is 5 one sixths.

items.narration: Count by halves. 1 half, 2 halves. Two halves make 1 whole. Move the frog to 2 halves.
items.why: Each half is 1/2. Two halves fill one whole, so the frog goes to 1.

items.narration: Count by thirds: 1/3, 2/3. What comes next? Is it 3/3, 4/3, or 2/4?
items.why: Each count adds one more third. After 2/3 comes 3/3, and 3/3 is one whole.

items.narration: A strip is cut into fifths. How many one fifths make 1 whole? Is it 4, 6, 5, or 10?
items.why: Fifths mean 5 equal parts. So 5 one fifths make 1 whole.

items.narration: Rosa adds 1/6 five times. The total is a fraction with 6 on the bottom. What number is on top?
items.why: The top number counts the pieces. Adding 1/6 five times gives 5 one sixths, which is 5/6.

items.narration: Two pizzas are each cut into 3 equal slices. Five slices are picked. Count the picked slices as one thirds. What fraction is that? Is it 3/5, 2/3, 5/3, or 6/5?
items.why: Count the picked slices: 5. Each slice is 1/3. So 5 one thirds is 5/3.

items.narration: Count by halves up to 5 halves. That is 5 × 1/2. Move the frog to 5 halves.
items.why: Two halves make 1 whole. Five halves is 2 wholes and 1 more half, so the frog lands on 2 and a half.

items.narration: Two bars are each cut into fourths. All the pieces are picked. How many one fourths are picked in all?
items.why: Each bar has 4 one fourths. Two bars have 4 + 4 = 8 one fourths.

items.narration: Adding 1/3 four times is 4 × 1/3. What fraction is that? Is it 3/4, 1/12, 4/3, or 4/4?
items.why: Four one thirds is 4/3. The count goes on top and the size of the piece goes on the bottom.

items.narration: Mia has 2 whole pizzas, each cut into 3 slices. She also has 1 more slice. How many one thirds does she have?
items.why: Each pizza is 3 one thirds. Two pizzas make 6, and 1 more makes 7 one thirds.

items.narration: Count by fifths. Move the frog to 9 × 1/5. That is 9 fifths, more than 1 whole.
items.why: Five fifths make 1 whole. Nine fifths is 1 whole and 4 more fifths, so the frog goes to 1.8.

items.narration: Each amount is 5 pieces of the same kind. Which is greatest: 5 × 1/4, 5 × 1/6, 5 × 1/3, or 5 × 1/8?
items.why: Fewer cuts make bigger pieces. Thirds are the biggest pieces here, so 5 × 1/3 is greatest.

items.narration: Leo has 9/4 of a bar, shown in the picture. He wants 3 whole bars. How many more one fourths does he need?
items.why: 3 whole bars is 3 × 4 = 12 one fourths. Leo has 9, so he needs 12 - 9 = 3 more.

items.narration: Is 6 × 1/5 more than 1 whole? Yes or no?
items.why: Six one fifths is 6/5. Five fifths make 1 whole, so 6/5 is 1 whole and 1 more fifth. Yes.

items.narration: A ten-frame is one whole. Seven dots are filled. Is that 0.3, 0.7, 1.7, or 7?
items.why: The frame has 10 parts. Seven are filled, so that is 7 tenths. As a decimal, 7 tenths is 0.7.

items.narration: Which is greater, 0.8 or 0.3?
items.why: Both are less than 1 whole. 8 tenths is more than 3 tenths. So 0.8 is greater.

items.narration: A ten-frame is one whole. Four dots are filled. Type the decimal for the filled part.
items.why: The frame has 10 parts and 4 are filled. That is 4 tenths. As a decimal, it is 0.4.

items.narration: Type the decimal for 9 tenths.
items.why: Tenths go right after the decimal point. No wholes means we start with 0. So 9 tenths is 0.9.

items.narration: Move the frog to 0.5 on the number line.
items.why: The line goes from 0 to 1 in 10 steps. Each step is one tenth. Count 5 steps from 0 to land on 0.5.

items.narration: Look at the number 24.7. What does the 7 mean? Is it 7 ones, 7 tenths, 7 tens, or 7 hundreds?
items.why: The 7 is the first digit after the dot. That place counts tenths. So the 7 means 7 tenths.

items.narration: Mia ran 3 whole laps and 5 tenths of another lap. Type her distance as a decimal.
items.why: The 3 wholes go before the dot. The 5 tenths go after it. So the number is 3.5.

items.narration: Look at 48.6. What digit is in the tenths place? Type that digit.
items.why: The tenths place is the first spot after the dot. In 48.6, the tenths digit is 6. So the 6 counts 6 tenths.

items.narration: This number line goes from 0 to 2. Move the frog to 1.4.
items.why: Start at 1. Then count 4 tenths more. That lands on 1.4.

items.narration: This number line goes from 4 to 5. Move the frog to 4.8.
items.why: The line starts at 4. Each step is one tenth. Count 8 steps from 4 to reach 4.8.

items.narration: Which is greatest, 7.5, 5.7, 7.1, or 5.9?
items.why: Compare the wholes first. 7 is more than 5, so it is 7.5 or 7.1. Then compare tenths. 5 tenths beats 1 tenth, so 7.5 is greatest.

items.narration: Is 2.0 the same as 2? Yes or no?
items.why: The 0 in the tenths place means no tenths. So 2.0 is 2 wholes and nothing more. It is the same as 2.

items.narration: A tank holds 12 tenths of a litre. Type that amount as a decimal.
items.why: 10 tenths make 1 whole. 12 tenths is 1 whole and 2 more tenths. So it is 1.2.

items.narration: This number line goes from 10 to 12. Move the frog to 11.3.
items.why: Start at 11. Then count 3 tenths more. That lands on 11.3.

items.narration: This number line goes from 24 to 26. Each step is two tenths. Move the frog to 25.4.
items.why: Start at 25. Then 4 tenths more is two jumps of 0.2. That lands on 25.4.

items.narration: Sam painted 1/2 of a fence. Which decimal is the same amount: 0.2, 0.5, 1.5, or 0.1?
items.why: One half is 5 out of 10 equal parts. Five tenths is written as 0.5.

items.narration: A ten-frame has 7 dots out of 10 spots. Type the decimal for 7 tenths.
items.why: Each dot is one tenth. Seven dots make 7 tenths, and the decimal is 0.7.

items.narration: Move the frog to 3/10 on the number line.
items.why: The line from 0 to 1 has 10 equal jumps. Count 3 jumps from 0 to land on 0.3.

items.narration: Which fraction is the same as 0.4: 1/10, 4/10, 6/10, or 10/4?
items.why: The digit after the dot counts tenths. The 4 means 4 tenths, so 0.4 is 4/10.

items.narration: How many tenths make 1 whole? Type the number.
items.why: A whole fence has 10 boards, and each board is one tenth. So 10 tenths make 1 whole.

items.narration: Move the frog to 15 tenths on the number line.
items.why: 15 tenths is 1 whole and 5 tenths more. That is 1.5, halfway between 1 and 2.

items.narration: Maya ran 6/10 of a kilometre. Which decimal is the same: 0.6, 6, 1.6, or 0.4?
items.why: Six tenths means 6 in the tenths place. So 6/10 is 0.6.

items.narration: How many tenths are in 1.3? Type the number of tenths.
items.why: 1 whole is 10 tenths. Add 3 more tenths to get 13 tenths.

items.narration: Is 7/10 the same amount as 0.07? Yes or no?
items.why: The first digit after the dot is tenths. So 7 tenths is 0.7, not 0.07.

items.narration: A dime is 1/10 of a dollar. Zoe has 3 dimes. Type that part of a dollar as a decimal.
items.why: Each dime is one tenth of a dollar. Three dimes are 3 tenths, which is 0.3.

items.narration: Which fraction is the same as 1.3: 3/10, 13/10, 1/3, or 31/10?
items.why: 1.3 is 1 whole and 3 tenths. One whole is 10 tenths, so that is 13 tenths.

items.narration: Move the frog to 24 tenths on the number line.
items.why: 24 tenths is 2 wholes, which is 20 tenths, plus 4 more tenths. That lands on 2.4.

items.narration: A rope is 2 and 7 tenths metres long. Type its length as a decimal.
items.why: The 2 wholes go before the dot. The 7 tenths go after the dot. That makes 2.7.

items.narration: Move the frog to 4/5 on the number line. Think about tenths.
items.why: Two fifths match 4 tenths, so each fifth is 2 tenths. Four fifths are 8 tenths, or 0.8.

items.narration: Which fraction is the same as 1.5: 1/5, 5/10, 2/3, or 3/2?
items.why: 1.5 is 15 tenths, which is 1 whole and a half. Three halves is also 1 whole and a half.

items.narration: What is 4 × 3?
items.why: Start with 2 × 3, which is 6. Double 6 is 12. So 4 × 3 is 12.

items.narration: 2 × 8 is 16. Double 16 to find 4 × 8. Is it 24, 32, 36, or 40?
items.why: 4 × 8 is double 2 × 8. Double 16 is 32.

items.narration: Move the frog to 4 × 6.
items.why: 2 × 6 is 12. Double 12 is 24. Hop to 24.

items.narration: What is 30 ÷ 6? Is it 3, 4, 5, or 6?
items.why: Think of the partner fact. 5 × 6 is 30, so 30 ÷ 6 is 5.

items.narration: Mia puts 18 stickers into 3 equal groups. How many stickers are in each group?
items.why: Think 3 times what is 18. 3 × 6 is 18, so 18 ÷ 3 is 6.

items.narration: What is 8 × 4?
items.why: 4 × 8 is double double 8. Double 8 is 16, and double 16 is 32.

items.narration: Sam knows 5 × 8 is 40. Add one more 8. What is 6 × 8? Is it 42, 46, 48, or 54?
items.why: 6 × 8 is 5 × 8 plus one more 8. 40 plus 8 is 48.

items.narration: Move the frog to 9 × 6.
items.why: 10 × 6 is 60. Take away one 6 to get 54.

items.narration: What is 56 ÷ 7? Is it 8, 7, 6, or 9?
items.why: Use the partner fact. 8 × 7 is 56, so 56 ÷ 7 is 8.

items.narration: A coach has 48 water bottles. She puts 8 bottles in each box. How many boxes does she need?
items.why: Think 8 times what is 48. 6 × 8 is 48, so she needs 6 boxes.

items.narration: What is 7 × 8?
items.why: Try 7 × 8 as 7 × 5 plus 7 × 3. That is 35 plus 21, which is 56.

items.narration: 72 players make teams of 8. How many teams are there? Is it 8, 12, 7, or 9?
items.why: Think 8 times what is 72. 9 × 8 is 72, so there are 9 teams.

items.narration: Sam has 9 boxes with 8 balls in each box. Move the frog to the number of balls.
items.why: 10 × 8 is 80. Take away one 8 to get 72.

items.narration: What number times 6 makes 54?
items.why: Use division. 54 ÷ 6 is 9, because 9 × 6 is 54.

items.narration: Which is greatest, 6 × 7, 5 × 9, 8 × 6, or 4 × 10?
items.why: 6 × 7 is 42, 5 × 9 is 45, 8 × 6 is 48, and 4 × 10 is 40. So 8 × 6 is greatest.
